flashcards.q: Why does transfer learning work — what do early vs late layers of a pretrained network actually learn?
flashcards.a: Hierarchical feature reuse: early layers learn general, broadly reusable patterns (edges, subword co-occurrence); late layers compose those into task-specific representations. Reusing general early layers means the target task only needs data to relearn the specific mapping, not the whole hierarchy.

flashcards.q: You have 800 labeled examples for a task close to the base model's pretraining domain. Where on the adaptation spectrum do you start?
flashcards.a: Frozen-feature extraction (freeze the base, train only a new head) or small-rank PEFT. Full fine-tuning on 800 examples risks overfitting and catastrophic forgetting.

flashcards.q: What is the observable symptom of catastrophic forgetting?
flashcards.a: A model fine-tuned on a narrow task suddenly fails at general capabilities it had before fine-tuning — e.g. a support-ticket classifier can no longer answer a general-knowledge question it used to get right. Caught via a held-out general-capability eval run before and after fine-tuning.

flashcards.q: How do discriminative (layer-wise) learning rates reduce catastrophic forgetting?
flashcards.a: They assign smaller learning rates to early (general-feature) layers and larger rates to late (task-specific) layers, typically via multiplicative decay per layer group (~0.9-0.95), so general features move minimally while task-specific layers adapt fully.

flashcards.q: State the 'dark knowledge' argument for why soft targets beat hard labels in distillation.
flashcards.a: A hard label says one class is right and all others are equally wrong. A teacher's full probability distribution encodes real similarity structure between classes (e.g. an ambiguous '2' getting P(2)=0.7, P(7)=0.25) that a one-hot label discards entirely — that structure is extra supervisory signal (Hinton et al., 2015).

flashcards.q: Write the knowledge distillation loss and explain the T^2 term.
flashcards.a: L = alpha * T^2 * KL(softmax_T(teacher) || softmax_T(student)) + (1-alpha) * CE(hard_label, student). T^2 corrects for softmax_T's gradient shrinking roughly as 1/T^2 as temperature rises, so the KL term's contribution isn't numerically drowned out at high T.

flashcards.q: What does temperature do in distillation, and what happens at T=1?
flashcards.a: Temperature softens (flattens) the teacher's output distribution so the useful signal in small probabilities over wrong classes becomes numerically visible instead of being drowned out by an overconfident near-one-hot softmax. At T=1 you're using the raw softmax, which degenerates distillation toward plain supervised learning on the teacher's argmax.

flashcards.q: Give DistilBERT's compression and retention numbers.
flashcards.a: ~97% of BERT-base's GLUE average (77.0 vs 79.5), at 40% smaller (66M vs 110M params) and roughly 60% faster inference on CPU.

flashcards.q: Give TinyBERT-4's compression and retention numbers, and what technique lets it compress harder than DistilBERT.
flashcards.a: 7.5x smaller (14.5M params), 9.4x faster, ~96.8% of BERT-base's GLUE average. It uses two-stage feature-level distillation (matching hidden states and attention matrices, not just final logits), giving a richer per-layer training signal than DistilBERT's response-only distillation.

flashcards.q: Name the three types of knowledge distillation by what's matched between teacher and student.
flashcards.a: Response distillation (final output logits/probabilities only), feature distillation (intermediate hidden states / attention matrices), and relation distillation (relationships between examples, e.g. pairwise similarity, rather than any single example's output).

flashcards.q: What is the licensing constraint that actually threatens real-world distillation projects?
flashcards.a: Most frontier providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, xAI) have anti-competitive-distillation clauses in their terms of service prohibiting use of model outputs to train a competing model. This is not hypothetical — it is the substance of a real, public OpenAI-vs-DeepSeek dispute alleging ToS violation via output extraction at scale.

flashcards.q: When is distillation the wrong call?
flashcards.a: When you already have enough labeled data to fine-tune the small student directly (skip the teacher-management overhead), when the task exceeds the student's capacity regardless of teacher quality (compression has a floor), or when there's no latency/cost pressure justifying the engineering investment (low QPS: just ship the big model).

flashcards.q: How do PEFT (e.g. LoRA) and knowledge distillation differ in what problem they solve?
flashcards.a: PEFT adapts one existing model to a new task by training small additional parameters while freezing the base — it's a fine-tuning technique. Distillation transfers capability from one model into a different, smaller architecture — it's a compression technique. They compose: fine-tune a large model first, then distill it into a small deployed model.

flashcards.q: How do you distill from a hosted frontier LLM you only access via API (no logit access)?
flashcards.a: Sequence-level distillation: generate a large volume of (input, teacher-generation) pairs and supervised-fine-tune the student on the teacher's generated text as the target. This loses the dark-knowledge benefit since you don't have the teacher's token-level probability distribution, and it may violate the provider's ToS if the teacher is a competing service.
